Statistical inference begins by naming the collection to which a claim refers. We call this requirement the **population-unit requirement** (PUR): a population is not defined until its units and their route into the data have been stated.

## A finite linguistic population

We begin with [UD Turkish BOUN, release 2.18](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/), a Universal Dependencies treebank for Turkish, a Turkic language. Türk et al. ([2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0)) describe the source and annotation process, while Marşan et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782)) document the agglutination-sensitive revisions. The release contains written sentences sampled within five selected Turkish National Corpus registers. Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed material.

The teaching extract contains each token tagged `UPOS=PRON` and `PronType=Prs` with an attested UD `Case` value. One row is one annotated token nested in a sampled sentence. The release is CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream permission conditions described in the [Turkish National Corpus paper](https://aclanthology.org/L12-1590/).

```{r}
#| label: load-ud-population
library(ggplot2)

pronouns <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/personal-pronoun-cases.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

case_counts <- as.data.frame(table(case = pronouns$case))
names(case_counts)[2] <- "tokens"
case_counts$proportion <- case_counts$tokens / sum(case_counts$tokens)
case_counts <- case_counts[order(case_counts$tokens), ]

stopifnot(
  nrow(pronouns) == 2128L,
  length(unique(pronouns$sentence_id)) == 1727L,
  sum(pronouns$accusative) == 430L
)

case_counts
```

This table is a census of the qualifying rows in one pinned release. It is not a probability sample of all Turkish personal-pronoun uses.

## Defining the objects

A **target population** is the collection of units about which an inference is intended. A **sample** is the collection observed through a particular selection process. A fixed numerical feature of a modeled population is a **parameter**; the rule used to calculate a candidate value from a sample is an **estimator**; and its realized value is an **estimate**.

For a binary indicator $X_i$ that equals one when token $i$ bears `Case=Acc`, the finite-release proportion is

$$
p_{\mathcal R}
=\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal R}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal R}}X_i,
$$

where $\mathcal R$ denotes this release and $N_{\mathcal R}$ is its number of qualifying token rows. The code computes that finite-population parameter directly.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-ud-population
release_size <- nrow(pronouns)
accusative_tokens <- sum(pronouns$accusative)
release_accusative_proportion <- mean(pronouns$accusative)

data.frame(
  qualifying_tokens = release_size,
  sentences_represented = length(unique(pronouns$sentence_id)),
  registers = length(unique(pronouns$register)),
  accusative_tokens = accusative_tokens,
  accusative_proportion = release_accusative_proportion
)
```

Thus $p_{\mathcal R}=$ `r sprintf("%.4f", release_accusative_proportion)` for the pinned release. There is no sampling uncertainty about this arithmetic once the release and filtering rule are fixed.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-cases
#| fig-cap: "Case counts among personal-pronoun tokens in UD Turkish BOUN 2.18."
ggplot(case_counts, aes(tokens, reorder(case, tokens))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.72) +
  labs(x = "Personal-pronoun tokens", y = "UD Case value") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## The route into the release

The source design matters. Approximately two thousand sentences were sampled within each of five selected written registers, and tokens are nested within those sentences. Thus a token-level analysis has more rows than sampled sentences, while neither count makes the registers a random sample of Turkish registers.

Two different claims consequently require different targets:

1. The finite-release claim concerns the qualifying annotated tokens in BOUN 2.18. The code above identifies its parameter exactly.
2. A usage claim concerns tokens that could arise from a specified Turkish production process. Connecting the release to that process requires a sampling model and assumptions about registers, sentences, and annotation.

This distinction is not repaired by a large row count. More token rows may yield a more precise description of the release while leaving its connection to Turkish usage unchanged.

## Check your understanding

1. What is the observational unit in `pronouns`, and what was the source selection unit?
2. Why is the computed proportion a parameter of the pinned release but only an estimate for a broader usage process?
3. Which identifiers reveal dependence among token rows?
4. What additional design information would be needed to generalize to spoken Turkish?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. One row is an annotated personal-pronoun token; the source design selected sentences within five written registers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The release and filter fix all qualifying rows, so the proportion is a known release parameter. A broader usage claim requires a sampling model, making the same quantity an estimate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Repeated `sentence_id` values show that token rows are nested within sentences; `register` also marks a shared source context. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. We would need a spoken-language sampling frame, selection probabilities for speakers and speech settings, and identifiers for speaker, conversation, and recording dependence. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](independent-sampling.qmd) states a working sampling model while keeping this unit hierarchy visible.
